concepts.name: Definition and Nature of Shruti as a Microtonal Unit
key_dimensions: Distinction between Shruti (microtone) and Swara (note) — a common UPSC trap
Etymology: 'Shruti' from Sanskrit root 'shru' (to hear) — the smallest perceptible interval
Shruti as a psychoacoustic concept vs. a fixed frequency measurement
Why Shruti cannot be sung in isolation unlike Swara

concepts.name: The Classical Count of 22 Shrutis in an Octave
key_dimensions: Textual authority: Bharata's Natyashastra as the primary source for 22-Shruti division
Why 22 and not 12 or 24 — the perceptual and mathematical basis
Comparison with Western 12-tone equal temperament and its implications
Controversy: whether 22 is an exact or approximate count across different theorists

concepts.name: Distribution of Shrutis Among the Seven Swaras (4-3-2-4-4-3-2 Pattern)
key_dimensions: Specific allocation: Sa(4), Re(3), Ga(2), Ma(4), Pa(4), Dha(3), Ni(2) — a direct factual question target
Why Sa and Pa receive 4 Shrutis each — their status as immovable (Achala) swaras
How this unequal distribution enables the variety of ragas
Trap: Sa itself does not 'move' but anchors the Shruti framework

concepts.name: Achala (Fixed) vs. Vikrita (Movable) Swaras in Shruti Framework
key_dimensions: Sa and Pa as Achala swaras — they have no flat or sharp variants in classical theory
The remaining 5 swaras as Vikrita — capable of occupying different Shruti positions
Implications for Raga construction: how Shruti position determines a note's character
Common UPSC trap: conflating 'Achala' with 'having no Shrutis' — they still occupy specific Shruti positions

concepts.name: Bharata Muni's Natyashastra and the Shruti System
key_dimensions: Natyashastra (2nd century BCE–2nd century CE) as the foundational text for Shruti theory
The 'Two Vina Experiment' described by Bharata to demonstrate Shruti differences
Bharata's classification of Shrutis into four types: Dipta, Ayata, Karuna, Mridu
Natyashastra's influence on both Hindustani and Carnatic traditions through later commentaries

concepts.name: The 'Two Vina Experiment' (Dvi-Vina Prayoga)
key_dimensions: Methodology: two Vinas tuned identically, then one detuned to isolate Shruti intervals
Its significance as possibly the world's earliest documented psychoacoustic experiment
What the experiment proves about human pitch perception vs. absolute frequency
Modern musicologists' debate on whether the experiment validates 22 or a different number of Shrutis

concepts.name: Four Qualitative Categories of Shrutis (Dipta, Ayata, Karuna, Mridu)
key_dimensions: Dipta (bright/sharp), Ayata (extended), Karuna (compassionate/soft), Mridu (tender) — their emotional associations
How these qualitative categories map onto the emotional theory of Rasa
The link between Shruti quality, emotional color, and Raga-Rasa correspondence
Trap: these are aesthetic/qualitative categories, NOT frequency measurements

concepts.name: Shruti vs. Swara: Conceptual Hierarchy and Interdependence
key_dimensions: Shruti as the 'position' or 'slot'; Swara as the 'note' that occupies a Shruti position
Multiple Swaras can share adjacent Shruti positions (e.g., Komal Re and Tivra Sa edge cases)
How a Raga's identity is partly determined by which specific Shruti a Swara occupies
Historical shift: classical texts treat Shruti as primary; modern practice often focuses on Swara

concepts.name: Shruti in Hindustani vs. Carnatic Classical Music Traditions
key_dimensions: Common theoretical origin but divergent practical application post-medieval period
Carnatic system's 16 Shuddha Swaras and 72 Melakarta framework vs. Hindustani's more fluid approach
Gamaka (ornament) in Carnatic music as the primary vehicle for Shruti expression
Hindustani music's Meend and Andolan as Shruti-traversal techniques
Trap: both systems acknowledge 22 Shrutis theoretically but operationalize them differently

concepts.name: Shruti and the Concept of Gamaka (Ornamentation)
key_dimensions: Gamaka as the movement between Shrutis — grace notes, oscillations, slides
Why Shruti theory is inseparable from ornament theory in Indian classical music
Ten classical Gamakas listed in medieval texts and their Shruti basis
Carnatic Gamaka vs. Hindustani Meend — same Shruti principle, different execution

concepts.name: Raga Identity and Shruti Specificity
key_dimensions: How two ragas using the 'same notes' differ due to occupying different Shruti positions (e.g., Bhairavi vs. Todi)
The concept of 'Vadi' and 'Samvadi' swaras and their Shruti-consonance relationship
Shruti as the microstructural basis explaining why certain note combinations are forbidden in specific ragas
Practical implication: a vocalist's intonation error at the Shruti level can change raga identity

concepts.name: Medieval Theorists and Evolution of Shruti Theory (Matanga, Sarangadeva, Venkatamakhi)
key_dimensions: Matanga's 'Brihaddeshi' (c. 9th century): transition from Gandharva to Desi music, Shruti contextualized
Sarangadeva's 'Sangita Ratnakara' (13th century): systematic elaboration of 22 Shrutis with mathematical ratios
Venkatamakhi's 'Chaturdandi Prakashika' (17th century): Carnatic systematization and Shruti-Melakarta linkage
UPSC trap: attributing Natyashastra concepts to later authors or vice versa

concepts.name: Mathematical Basis of Shrutis: Ratios and Just Intonation
key_dimensions: Shrutis expressed as frequency ratios (e.g., 256/243, 16/15) — the 'just intonation' system
Comparison with Pythagorean tuning and equal temperament — why Indian system resists standardization
The 'syntonic comma' and 'Pythagorean comma' as Western equivalents of Shruti differences
Why standardization of Shrutis to fixed Hz values is considered contrary to the spirit of the system

concepts.name: Shruti in the Context of Nada (Sound) Philosophy
key_dimensions: Nada Brahma concept: sound as cosmic principle — Shruti as its most refined perceptible unit
Anahata Nada (unstruck sound) vs. Ahata Nada (struck sound) and where Shruti fits
Philosophical texts (Sangita Ratnakara) linking Shruti to breath (Prana) and cosmic vibration
Trap: Nada philosophy is metaphysical; Shruti theory is both philosophical AND technical — distinguish contexts

concepts.name: Shruti Instruments: The Shruti Box and Tanpura's Role
key_dimensions: Tanpura as the primary drone instrument that sustains the Shruti framework during performance
The Shruti Box (electronic/manual) as a modern pedagogical tool — its limitations vs. Tanpura
How the harmonic overtones of Tanpura reinforce specific Shrutis and define the tonal space of a raga
The Veena's frets historically positioned to access specific Shrutis — fixed fret vs. unfretted instrument debate

concepts.name: Shruti in UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage Context and Modern Preservation
key_dimensions: Oral transmission (Guru-Shishya Parampara) as the primary vehicle for Shruti knowledge — not written notation
Challenges of notating Shruti differences in Western staff notation or Indian Sargam
Digital musicology initiatives (IIT research, SaPaDa project) attempting to map Shrutis acoustically
UNESCO recognition of Hindustani and Carnatic traditions — Shruti knowledge as intangible heritage

concepts.name: Shruti and the Concept of Sruthi-Bedha (Transposition by Shruti Shift)
key_dimensions: Murchhana: the ancient system of generating new scales by shifting the starting Shruti point
How Shruti-Bedha (changing the Sa to a different Shruti position) theoretically generates all ragas
Relation to the modern concept of 'modal shift' in Western music theory
Trap: Murchhana is NOT the same as modulation in Western classical music — key distinctions

concepts.name: Shruti Perception and Psychoacoustics: Cross-Cultural Comparisons
key_dimensions: Scientific studies (Jairazbhoy, Levy) measuring whether trained Indian musicians actually sing 22 distinct pitches
Comparison with Arabic Maqam quarter-tones and Turkish makam microtones — convergence and divergence
The role of cultural conditioning in Shruti perception — why Western-trained ears may not distinguish them
UPSC angle: India's contribution to world music theory through microtonal systems predating Western acoustics

concepts.name: Shruti in Vedic Recitation vs. Shruti in Classical Music — Terminological Overlap
key_dimensions: Shruti as 'that which is heard' = Vedic texts (Sruti/Scripture) — a completely different usage
Three Vedic accents: Udatta, Anudatta, Svarita — these are NOT musical Shrutis but a common confusion point
How Vedic recitation tonality may have historically influenced early Shruti theory development
Critical UPSC trap: 'Shruti' in music ≠ 'Shruti' as sacred texts — questions may exploit this ambiguity

concepts.name: Contemporary Relevance: Shruti in Fusion Music and Digital Age Challenges
key_dimensions: Collision of Shruti-based tuning with equal-tempered instruments (piano, guitar) in fusion performances
Pandit Ravi Shankar's and Ustad Ali Akbar Khan's navigation of Shruti system in global collaborations
Software tools (like Audacity, specialized ragas apps) attempting to digitize Shruti maps
Policy relevance: Music education curriculum debate — whether NCERT/Sangeet Natak Akademi should standardize Shruti notation
